titre: The First Spam in History Didn't Have a Name Yet
accroche: On May 3, 1978, a marketing manager sent the same message to hundreds of people on a network reserved for research. The word “spam” doesn't exist yet.
contenu_vulgarise:
On May 3, 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketing manager at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), wanted to announce two open-house events, in Los Angeles and San Mateo, where his company would unveil its latest computers, the DECSYSTEM-20. Rather than write one message per recipient, he chose to write a single one for everyone. The message, sent from his account by engineer Carl Gartley, went out to about 393 addresses on ARPANET, the network that would become the Internet, which at the time had barely 2,600 addresses in total. The word “spam” doesn't exist yet to describe this kind of mailing: it would take until the 1980s, and then 1994, before it took on that meaning.

## A research network, not a marketplace

In 1978, ARPANET was neither a public utility nor a commercial space: it was a network funded by the U.S. military, reserved for research and government business. Advertising on it broke its usage rules, and the reaction was swift. Recipients, mostly researchers and administrators, protested in large numbers; network officials reprimanded Thuerk and made him promise not to do it again. Decades later, in an interview, Thuerk openly claimed credit for his move: “I was the pioneer,” he would say. “I saw a new way of doing things.” He would also claim that the campaign generated, in his own words, thirteen to fourteen million dollars in sales for DEC, and that he never had to repeat the move.

## An act with no word to describe it

What makes this episode unusual is that it predates, by several years, the very vocabulary that would describe it. The word “spam” comes from a sketch on the British television series Monty Python's Flying Circus, aired in 1970, in which a waitress reads out a menu where almost every dish contains Spam, a brand of canned meat, while a chorus of Vikings drowns out the conversation by repeating the word. In the 1980s, on early chat forums and online games (BBSs and MUDs), users picked up the word to describe people who flooded others' screens by repeating the same text over and over. The term then drifted onto Usenet, where it came to mean the mass reposting of the same message across many discussion groups, as in the notorious “Green Card spam” of March 5, 1994, which truly ushered in the age of mass commercial spam. It wasn't until 1998 that the New Oxford Dictionary of English finally added this sense of the word. Thuerk's 1978 message is thus spam before the letter, in the most literal sense: the act already existed; no one yet had a word to name it, or a reflex to filter it. The only defense available at the time wasn't technical but social: a reprimand, which, according to an Internet historian quoted in the press, probably delayed for several years the rise of the very practice this message had just inaugurated.

carte.punch: The first spam in history dates to 1978. The word “spam” didn't exist yet.
carte.idee: In 1978, a marketing manager sent the same ad to hundreds of addresses on ARPANET, a network then reserved for research. Administrators reprimanded him. The word to describe that act, borrowed from a Monty Python sketch, wouldn't take on this meaning for another sixteen years.

quiz.question: Why wasn't the message Gary Thuerk sent in 1978 called “spam” at the time?
choix: Because the word didn't yet have that meaning: it would only take it on in later years
Because the message was ultimately blocked before reaching its recipients
Because ARPANET's official rules forbade the use of that word
Because Thuerk worked for DEC rather than for a messaging company
quiz.explication: The word “spam” comes from a Monty Python sketch (1970), was adopted in the 1980s to describe a flood of repeated messages, then extended on Usenet to mass reposting, before entering a dictionary only in 1998. In 1978, Thuerk's act already existed; the word to name it didn't yet.
